opus-5.5.text:
I think the main problem is that a job isn't really a single, well-defined thing. When you look at what people actually do over the course of a week, a job is a bundle of many different tasks, and those tasks can be very heterogeneous. Some of them might be quite easy to automate with current systems, and some might be very hard. So if you ask "will AI automate this job?", you're kind of asking about the hardest task in the bundle, or at least about whether the bundle can be reorganized so that the hard parts get split off and handed to someone else.

And that reorganization is the other big issue. Historically, when automation comes in, jobs don't just disappear wholesale. What usually happens is that the task composition of the job shifts. Some tasks get automated, the remaining ones become a larger share of what the worker does, and sometimes entirely new tasks get added. Think about how much of what a secretary or a bank teller did fifty years ago has been automated, yet the occupations didn't vanish overnight. They changed shape. So if you analyze at the level of the job title, you can miss most of the action. You might conclude nothing is happening when actually a huge fraction of the underlying work has been automated, or conversely you might predict a job will vanish when really it'll just be restructured.

So I find it more useful to think at the level of tasks, and then to ask what fraction of the economically valuable tasks in the economy AI can perform, and at what cost. That's a much cleaner variable to reason about. The job-level picture then falls out of how firms choose to bundle the remaining tasks together, which depends on things like coordination costs and complementarities between tasks, and that's genuinely hard to predict in advance.

There's also a measurement point. Occupational categories are defined by statistical agencies for their own purposes, and they're fairly coarse. Two people with the same job title can be doing quite different work. So even empirically, if you try to track automation through employment in particular occupations, you get a noisy and lagging signal. By the time an occupation visibly shrinks, the task-level automation has often been going on for a long time.

The one place where the job-level framing does matter is at the very end. If AI gets to the point where it can do essentially all the tasks, including the ones that require long-horizon planning, coordination, and adapting to unfamiliar situations, then whole jobs do go away, because there's no residual bundle left for a human to specialize in. But getting there is precisely the question of whether those last, hardest tasks fall, and that's again a task-level question. So in both the intermediate and the end-state cases, I think tasks are the right unit of analysis.

r001.rationale: The response says jobs bundle many heterogeneous tasks, but it does not clearly state that they combine multiple different skills.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the main issue is that a job isn't really a natural unit of analysis for what AI is actually doing. A job is a bundle of tasks that happen to be grouped together for one person, and the grouping reflects historical contingencies, organizational structure, what's convenient for a firm to hire for, and so on. It's not something that corresponds to a particular level of capability.

So when you ask "can AI automate this job," you're really asking a question about dozens of heterogeneous tasks at once, and the answer is almost always "some of them, not others." Take something like a software engineer. There's writing code, but there's also understanding what the customer actually wants, coordinating with other people, debugging production systems, making judgment calls about tradeoffs. Current systems are very good at some of those and quite bad at others. If you try to say yes or no at the level of the whole job, you lose all the interesting structure.

And the other problem is that jobs themselves change in response to automation. Historically, when part of a job gets automated, the job doesn't disappear; it gets redefined around whatever's left. So the thing you were trying to predict shifts under you. Bank tellers after ATMs, or accountants after spreadsheets. The occupation persisted, but the task composition changed a lot.

That's why I tend to prefer thinking at the task level, or even more abstractly in terms of what capabilities are required: how long a horizon the task has, how much context it needs, how legible the success criteria are. Those dimensions give you something you can actually track over time as models improve. Whereas "jobs automated" is a measure where the denominator keeps moving and the categories don't map cleanly onto anything the technology is doing.

The caveat is that for economic questions, jobs do matter, because that's how labor markets are organized and that's what people experience. So you eventually have to aggregate back up. But I think you want to do the analysis at the task level first and then ask how tasks recombine, rather than starting from job titles.

r001.rationale: The response says jobs bundle heterogeneous tasks and gives examples of different capabilities within software engineering, explaining why a whole-job yes/no judgment is difficult.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difficulty is that a job is a bundle of quite different tasks. Some might be easy to automate, while others are much harder. So if you ask, “Can AI do this job?” you’re compressing a lot of variation into a single yes-or-no question.

And automating some of those tasks doesn’t necessarily mean the job disappears. It might mean that a person can do much more work, or that they spend more of their time on the parts that still need human input. The job itself changes as the technology improves.

So I think it’s more useful to start at the level of tasks and then ask how automating those tasks affects the way work is organized. Even there, you have to consider how the tasks fit together. Being able to do most of a job isn’t necessarily enough to replace someone if the remaining part is essential.

r001.rationale: The response says jobs bundle different tasks, but it does not say that jobs combine multiple different skills.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difficulty is that a job is a bundle of different tasks, and those tasks can vary quite a lot even between people who have the same job title. So if you ask, “Can AI automate the work of a lawyer?” it’s not clear exactly what you mean. Do you mean doing legal research, drafting documents, talking to clients, or appearing in court? Those are quite different capabilities.

And automating some of those tasks doesn’t necessarily mean that you can automate the whole job. You might make a lawyer much more productive while still needing a person to handle certain parts of the work. Conversely, once some tasks are automated, firms can reorganize the work, so the bundle of tasks that makes up the job changes.

So I find it more useful to start at the level of tasks and then ask how those changes translate into demand for human labor. You can’t just take the fraction of tasks an AI can do and interpret that as the fraction of jobs that will disappear.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a job bundles different tasks requiring different capabilities, making whole-job automation difficult to assess.
